title: The Rooftop Laundry Code
markdown:
Dawn kicked gold across the tiles. Pinks and tangerines burst along the chimney pots. Nix the rooftop rat stood on the ridge and felt the city tick. Today had a different beat. Cool air. Bread ovens starting. Pigeons arguing. Secrets, if you knew how to look.

Nix knew. Cracks, flight-lines, laundry: he read them the way other rats read crumbs. People were messier. People changed their minds. He kept to roofs.

Then he saw the line.

Sheets hung in a run that was not random: red, blue, yellow, stripe, blue, polka dot. Nix’s heart hammered. A code. A big one. It smelled like a prank, and the bucket above the park gate was already tipping on its string. The kind park keeper would walk under it at noon. Nix had until then.

“Brilliant,” he squeaked, and dashed.

Sorrel the black cat slept on a warm slate, one emerald eye shut on principle. “Sorrel. Wake up. Puzzle. Urgent.”

The eye opened a slit. “Nix. Sunrise. Croissant.”

“Bigger than croissants. Laundry is talking.”

Sorrel yawned, a pink cave of tidy teeth. “Laundry. Speaking. Sleep, Nix.” She stretched and closed the eye again.

Nix’s whiskers drooped. Too small. Too quiet. He stared at a scatter of leaves: red, brown, yellow, brown, red. His voice stuck.

Wings clapped. Edan the pigeon dropped onto the ridge. “Secrets? And washing?”

Nix popped upright. “Edan. Look. Red, blue, yellow, stripe, blue, polka dot.”

Edan tipped his head. “Signal flags. Uncle Percy taught me. One bad knot once declared war on the ducks.”

“What does it say?”

“Red is danger. Blue is proceed. Yellow is caution. Stripe is divert.” Edan puffed. “Polka dot is the silly one. Falling acorns. Queen’s hat blown off. That sort of joke.”

“Silly stuff,” Nix said, and the pieces clicked. “They’re dressing a splash as an accident. The keeper. We stop it.”

Sorrel sat up so fast her tail drew a question mark. “The keeper? He leaves extra water. Fine. You lead, Nix.”

Warmth hit Nix like sun on tin. Allies. “Right. Go.”

They raced the lines. Nix pointed. Edan flapped between roofs and called the changes. Can you imagine trying to read flags that keep swapping?

“Blue is gone,” Edan shouted. “Plain white now!”

A gust slammed the yard. Soap-smell punched the air. Sheets cracked like banners. Nix’s mental map blew apart. “Notes. Gone.” Panic bubbled, then he bit it back.

Below, a terrier snapped at Sorrel’s tail. She leapt a gap and hissed, “Too close.”

“I saw the white,” Edan called, circling. “White is final action. Maximum splash.”

Nix breathed. Sorrel was taut. Edan was locked on. The first pattern was still in him if he trusted it. People were unpredictable. Friends, it turned out, could be a pattern too.

“Stripe means divert,” he said, firm now. “Polka dot means they want it to look like wind. Move the red shirt. Park it on the chimney. Drop the blue pillowcase where the red was.”

Sorrel sprang up the trellis. Edan butted the pillowcase into place. Nix shoved the red shirt until it snagged on a pot and hung there like a confession. The bucket’s string, tied to the old red, now tugged nothing useful.

Sparrows finished the last pegs, chuckling. The park keeper stepped out, whistling, reached for the gate —

Nothing fell. Laundry only swayed.

The sparrows squawked and left in a huff. Nix, Sorrel, and Edan grinned on the ridge. The same gold that had kicked the tiles now ran the whole street. Nix felt a fizz that was not only the solved code. He had used his head and their paws together. He had gone near people on purpose.

He flicked his tail toward the next block of washing, already twitching with a new sequence. “Breakfast,” he said. “Then we check the west roofs. Today is going to be packed.”

He dashed. Sorrel and Edan had to bounce to keep up.
characters: Nix (a rooftop rat), Sorrel (a sleek black cat), Edan (a signal pigeon)
